newsitem.title: UK: No-fly zone extension piles pressure on Saddam.
newsitem.headline: No-fly zone extension piles pressure on Saddam.

text.p: The Western allies decided on Tuesday to extend a no-fly zone in southern Iraq to within 30 miles (50 km) of Baghdad to further limit Saddam Hussein's ability to manoeuvre in his own country.

The one degree northwards extension of the so-called "safe haven", set up after the 1991 Gulf War to protect the marsh Arabs, will take effect at noon Baghdad time on Wednesday, British officials said.
The northern safe area protecting Kurds which extends to the border with Turkey will remain unaffected. The extension follows a U.S. missile attack on Iraqi targets on Tuesday.

"The no-fly zone in southern Iraq will be extended to allow the allies operating there to have a greater opportunity to control more of Saddam's airspace and bring greater control over him," said Defence Secretary Michael Portillo.

"He (Saddam) will not be pleased about the fact that a very large area of Iraq is not available for him to fly and that he is effectively denied the use of a number of important air bases in southern Iraq," Portillo added.

Most analysts expected military action would be limited to Tuesday's air attack on Iraqi installations in rural areas as punishment for Saddam's attack on the Kurdish city of Arbil, deep within the northern safe haven.
The extension of the southern safe haven zone was clearly intended to exert the greatest pressure on Saddam with the least military outlay for the West, they said.
No extra planes over and above those already used by France, Britain and the United States are envisaged to patrol the new, larger zone which will now reach up to the 33rd parallel.
"The proximity to Baghdad is obviously intended to have a psychological effect on Saddam," said Lawrence Freedman, professor of war studies at King's College.

"They could be warning Saddam of a much wider range of operation. The no-fly zone has no particular United Nations status...so they don't have to go back to the UN to do it. That is a third reason," Freedman told Reuters.

The safe havens in the north and south were set up to protect Iraq's Kurds and Shi'ite Moslems after they both staged failed revolts following the 1991 Gulf War. Iraqi civil and military planes are banned from entering the airspace.

The southern zone is enforced mainly by aircraft stationed in Saudi Arabia. Portillo acknowledged that the extension of the southern safe haven might have little effect on Iraqi advances on Kurdish areas in the north.
"This is not like the Gulf War. By January of that war hundreds of thousands of allied troops were out on the ground and we were able to intervene very effectively.
"We are not at that stage. We had to do what we can do with the assets that we have," Portillo told BBC television.
Britain however insisted the extension was a direct response to the Iraqi attack last week on the Kurdish city of Arbil.
Analyst Aile Saunders, head of the Middle East programme at the Royal United Services Institute, said there could also be a wider motive.

"It may also be an additional warning to the Iranians in case the Iranians think this is an opportunity to start a cross border operation, and being concerned that the Shi'ites in the south might invite them in," she said.
